title: How to Calculate Your Annual Base Salary from an Hourly Rate
description: Convert your hourly rate to an annual base salary using 38 hours per week. Includes National Minimum Wage, award rates, casual loading, tax, and super.
salarySummary: For a full-time employee working 38 hours per week, the annual base salary is the hourly rate multiplied by 38 hours and 52 weeks.

faqs.a: Annual base salary is the fixed amount of money you earn in a year before any additional payments such as overtime, bonuses, or superannuation. It is typically expressed as a gross figure and is calculated from your hourly rate multiplied by the number of hours you work per week and the number of weeks per year (usually 52). For full-time employees, the standard is 38 hours per week, as defined by the Fair Work Ombudsman. Your annual base salary does not include casual loading, penalty rates, or superannuation – those are paid on top.

faqs.q: How do I convert my hourly rate to an annual salary?
faqs.a: Multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work per week, then multiply by 52 weeks. For example, if you are a full-time employee on the National Minimum Wage of $26.44 per hour and work 38 hours per week, your annual base salary is $26.44 × 38 × 52 = $52,253.44. If you work fewer hours or are casual, adjust the weekly hours accordingly. Casual employees receive a 25% loading on top of the base hourly rate, so their effective hourly rate is higher, but the annual base salary calculation remains the same – the loading is added separately.

faqs.q: Does annual base salary include superannuation?
faqs.a: No, annual base salary does not include superannuation. Under the Superannuation Guarantee, your employer must pay an additional 12% of your ordinary earnings into a super fund, on top of your base salary. For the 2026–27 financial year, this contribution is capped at the maximum contribution base of $270,830. So if your annual base salary is $80,000, your employer pays an extra $9,600 in super, making your total remuneration $89,600. Always check your pay slip to confirm super is being paid separately.

bodyMarkdown:
## Understanding Your Annual Base Salary

Your **annual base salary** is the gross amount you earn in a year from your ordinary hours of work, before any extras like overtime, bonuses, or superannuation. It is the foundation of your pay package and the figure most commonly used in employment contracts and salary negotiations.

To convert an hourly rate to an annual base salary, use this simple formula:

**Annual base salary = hourly rate × hours per week × 52 weeks**

For full-time employees, the standard ordinary hours are 38 per week, as defined by the Fair Work Ombudsman. If you work a different number of hours – for example, part-time or under an enterprise agreement – use your actual weekly hours.

### From Hourly Rate to Annual Base Salary

Let’s take the National Minimum Wage (NMW) from 1 July 2026. The Fair Work Commission sets it at $26.44 per hour for a 38-hour week. That gives:

- **Weekly base pay:** $26.44 × 38 = $1,004.90
- **Fortnightly base pay:** $1,004.90 × 2 = $2,009.80
- **Annual base salary:** $26.44 × 38 × 52 = **$52,253.44**

This is the minimum annual base salary for an adult employee not covered by an award or agreement. Most employees, however, are covered by a modern award or enterprise agreement that sets higher minimum rates. Use our [pay guides](/blog) to find the correct award rate for your industry.

### The National Minimum Wage vs Award Rates

The NMW applies only to award/agreement-free employees. If you are covered by a modern award, your minimum hourly rate will be higher – often significantly. For example, the Hospitality Industry General Award or the Manufacturing Award have different classifications with their own rates. The Fair Work Ombudsman’s Pay and Conditions Tool can help you determine the correct rate. Our [reference tables](/data) also summarise common award classifications.

Even if you are paid above the award, your annual base salary is still calculated the same way: hourly rate × weekly hours × 52. The difference is that award rates may include allowances or penalty rates that are not part of the base salary calculation – those are added on top.

### Casual Loading and Annual Base Salary

Casual employees receive a 25% loading on top of the base hourly rate to compensate for not receiving paid leave. For the NMW, the casual rate is $26.44 × 1.25 = $33.05 per hour. However, the **annual base salary** is still calculated from the base rate, not the loaded rate. The loading is an additional payment.

When using our [the timesheet](/) calculator, you can check the “Casual loading” box to automatically add 25% to your hourly rate. This gives you the effective hourly pay, but remember that the annual base salary shown is based on the rate you enter – if you include the loading, the result will be higher than your true base salary. Always enter your base hourly rate (without loading) to see your correct annual base salary.

### Fortnightly and Weekly Pay

Many employers pay weekly or fortnightly. To find your weekly pay, multiply your hourly rate by your weekly hours. For fortnightly, double that figure. Using the NMW example:

- Weekly: $1,004.90
- Fortnightly: $2,009.80

If you are paid a salary, your pay slip should show your annual base salary. The Fair Work Ombudsman explains that annualised wages must cover all award entitlements and be reviewed each year.

### Tax and Superannuation

Your annual base salary is the starting point for tax and super calculations. For the 2026–27 financial year, the Australian Taxation Office’s resident tax rates are:

- $0 – $18,200: nil
- $18,201 – $45,000: 15% on excess over $18,200
- $45,001 – $135,000: 30% on excess over $45,000
- $135,001 – $190,000: 37% on excess over $135,000
- Over $190,000: 45% on excess over $190,000

Plus the Medicare levy of 2% (with possible reductions for low-income earners).

Superannuation is paid **on top** of your annual base salary. The Super Guarantee rate is 12% of your ordinary earnings, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830. So if your annual base salary is $80,000, your employer contributes an extra $9,600 to your super fund. This is not deducted from your salary – it is an additional cost to the employer.

Use our [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) calculator to estimate your net pay after tax and Medicare, and our [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging) guide to understand salary sacrifice options.

### Using the Timesheet

Our [the timesheet](/) tool lets you enter your base hourly rate and weekly hours (default 38). It instantly shows your annual base salary, fortnightly and weekly equivalents, and estimates tax and super. You can toggle casual loading to see the effect of the 25% loading. The results are estimates only – always check your employment contract or award for exact figures.

**Disclaimer:** Annual pay here is hourly rate × hours per week × 52. It assumes the same rate every week, no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, no allowances, and no salary sacrifice. Super is estimated at 30% of ordinary earnings only, paid on top, and stops at the $270,830 maximum contribution base. Tax is the 2026–27 resident scale with the full tax-free threshold. Medicare uses the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds because the 2027–27 reduction thresholds were not confirmed here. HELP, the Medicare levy surcharge, and salary packaging are not deducted. This is an estimate, not a determination of your pay or tax.
